extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of constitutional law, political science, and comparative government
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and practical rules for when U.S. federal courts (and the Supreme Court) have jurisdiction, plus related procedural devices and constitutional design features that affect how federal power is exercised and defended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supreme Court's authority to determine jurisdictional questions
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court of the United States was therefore invested with the right of determining all questions of jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because no neutral third tribunal could be created between federal and state superior courts, the Constitution (and practice) requires that one of the courts judge its own competency; the Supreme Court's role prevents conflicting state interpretations from undermining national supremacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basis of Federal Jurisdiction: matter and party
rubrics_metrics.description: The matter and the party are the first conditions of the Federal jurisdiction—certain parties must always be brought before the Federal courts, and certain causes must always be brought before the same courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jurisdiction is determined both by who the parties are (e.g., ambassadors, the Union, states, citizens of different states) and by the subject matter of the dispute (e.g., cases arising under U.S. laws, admiralty).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambassador suits belong in federal courts
rubrics_metrics.description: When an ambassador is a party in a suit, that suit affects the welfare of the nation, and a Federal tribunal is naturally called upon to decide it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because ambassadors represent nations in amity with the Union, suits involving them have national significance and should be decided by federal tribunals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suits to which the Union (federal government) is a party go to federal courts
rubrics_metrics.description: The Union itself may be invoked in legal proceedings, and ... it would be alike contrary to the customs of all nations and to common sense to appeal to a tribunal representing any other sovereignty than its own; the Federal courts, therefore, take cognizance of these affairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include enforcement of federal imposts and other federal laws where the national government is enforcing rights or obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversity jurisdiction (parties from different States)
rubrics_metrics.description: When two parties belonging to two different States are engaged in a suit, the case cannot with propriety be brought before a court of either State ... a tribunal like that of the Union ... offers the most natural as well as the most certain remedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diversity jurisdiction exists to avoid bias of a state court toward its own citizens; it is a party-based ground for federal jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suits between States are federal
rubrics_metrics.description: When the two parties are not private individuals, but States, an important political consideration is added ... the quality of the parties in this case gives a national importance to all their disputes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interstate suits implicate the peace of the whole Union and are thus properly heard by federal tribunals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal-question jurisdiction: cases arising under the laws of the United States
rubrics_metrics.description: The judicial power of the Supreme Court shall extend to all cases in law and equity arising under the laws of the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a case depends on the interpretation or validity of a federal statute or the Constitution (e.g., state law on currency, disputes about federal import duties), it falls within federal jurisdiction; examples: state laws on money or resistance to federal imposts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maritime, admiralty, and law-of-nations matters are federal
rubrics_metrics.description: All the questions which concern maritime commerce evidently fall under the cognizance of the Federal tribunals. Almost all these questions are connected with the interpretation of the law of nations ... Moreover, as the sea is not included within the limits of any peculiar jurisdiction, the national courts can only hear causes which originate in maritime affairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific examples include cases of piracy and other admiralty matters; these are federal because they implicate national and international law and lack state territorial attachment.

rubrics_metrics.name: State laws violating the Constitution (ex post facto, impairment of contracts) permit federal review
rubrics_metrics.description: The jurisdiction of the Federal courts extends not only to all the cases which arise under the laws of the Union, but also to those which arise under laws made by the several States in opposition to the Constitution ... The States are prohibited from making ex post facto laws in criminal cases ... The States are likewise prohibited from making laws which may have a tendency to impair the obligations of contracts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Individuals injured by state laws that violate constitutional prohibitions (e.g., ex post facto laws or laws impairing contracts) may appeal to federal courts; historical example: Dartmouth College charter treated as a contract and protected from state impairment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical device: enforce federal rights by bringing private individuals into federal courts
rubrics_metrics.description: The Constitution contrived ... that the federal courts, acting in the name of the laws, should only take cognizance of parties in an individual capacity ... the inference was that the Government ... was invested with all the privileges of a national government, one of the principal of which is the right of transmitting its injunctions directly to the private citizen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than suing a State directly (which is politically dangerous), the Union secures federal enforcement by applying federal law against private individuals (e.g., tax enforcement against taxpayers), thereby making federal authority effective while avoiding direct conflict with State sovereignty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect prosecution: attacking state laws via their consequences on private rights
rubrics_metrics.description: The Union chose its own antagonist; and as that antagonist is feeble, he is naturally worsted ... it attacks the law in its consequences, not in its principle, and it rather weakens than destroys it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: when a state passes an act impairing a contract concerning land, the aggrieved private party brings suit in federal court to have the state-created title set aside; federal courts thus remedy the effect of the state law without directly annulling the law as an abstract principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indispensability and political character of the Supreme Court
rubrics_metrics.description: A more imposing judicial power was never constituted ... Its power extends to all the cases arising under laws and treaties ... and in general to all points which affect the law of nations. It may even be affirmed that, although its constitution is essentially judicial, its prerogatives are almost entirely political.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Supreme Court enforces Union laws, protects the Union from state disobedience and guards the public interest; because its decisions affect vast political questions (including suits between large polities), the Court's discretion and character have profound national consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial independence: protections and required qualities of federal judges
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal Constitution ... carefully separates the judicial authority from all external influences; and it provides for the independence of the judges, by declaring that their salary shall not be altered, and that their functions shall be inalienable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal judges should be good citizens and statesmen — informed, patriotic, and able to resist improper encroachments. Their life-tenure-like protections and unalterable salary are intended to secure impartiality and courage in defending the Constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Longer legislative terms to reduce momentary dependence on popular passions
rubrics_metrics.description: The greater number of the Constitutions of the States assign one year for the duration of the House of Representatives ... The legislators of the Union were of opinion that this excessive dependence of the Legislature tended to alter the nature of the main consequences of the representative system; They increased the length of the time for which the representatives were returned, in order to give them freer scope for the exercise of their own judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Longer terms for federal legislators were designed to allow more deliberation and to insulate national lawmakers from short-term popular impulses that might produce hasty or turbulent legislation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate composition/selection as a check against transient popular passions
rubrics_metrics.description: A mature age was made one of the conditions of the senatorial dignity, and the Upper House was chosen by an elected assembly of a limited number of members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By altering conditions of eligibility and mode of selection for the Senate (relative to state legislatures), the Federal Constitution sought to have one chamber represent a 'superior degree of intelligence and discretion.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive independence within prescribed limits (four-year term, protected salary, suspensive veto)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal Constitution vests all the privileges and all the responsibility of the executive power in a single individual. The duration of the Presidency is fixed at four years; the salary ... cannot be altered during the term of his functions; he is protected by a body of official dependents, and armed with a suspensive veto.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These design choices create an executive able to resist fleeting popular pressure and legislative domination while remaining constrained by constitutional limits (suspensive veto, fixed term).
